paras: The threatened lynching of Law Young and William Murphey took place at Gladstone, Nelson County, Virginia, on September 11, 1903, when a crowd of several hundred gathered to await two Black men arrested on suspicion of killing a white man on a freight train. Authorities at Lynchburg, where the two were held, declined to send them to Gladstone, and no harm to them was reported. Another Black man, Frank Bradley, was later charged with the killing, convicted, and hanged.

Early on the morning of September 11, William P. Harris of Iron Gate was shot dead on a Chesapeake and Ohio freight train near Gladstone, twenty-five miles east of Lynchburg. Crew members heard pistol shots but found his body on a car only when the train reached Gladstone. Harris, described in a later report as a white bridge-builder, worked for the American Bridge Company in Richmond and was on his way to visit his wife and two children. His watch was missing, though money he carried was untouched.

Law Young and William Murphey, two Black men who had been at Gladstone when the body was found, were arrested at Lynchburg as they were "beating their way west." Both said they knew nothing of the shooting. According to a Lynchburg dispatch to the Richmond Times-Dispatch, there was "much excitement" at Gladstone, where a crowd of several hundred people waited through the day for the two men to arrive.

The Lynchburg authorities, the dispatch said, "would not incur the responsibility" of taking the prisoners to Gladstone, and arranged instead for a Gladstone official to collect them the next day. The report ended with the line "Trouble is feared." No account of the men's transfer to Gladstone, or of any attack on them, appears in the coverage.

On Saturday, September 12, Frank Bradley, a Black man, was arrested at Warminster and charged with the murder, and a Baldwin agency detective, C. D. Duke, brought him to the Henrico County jail. Duke said Bradley had ridden the freight with Harris after a night of drinking in Richmond and carried a revolver whose fired chambers had been reloaded; Bradley denied the killing and blamed a man in overalls. A Lynchburg dispatch of September 14 said Bradley had been with Young and Murphy, "who have been arrested for the crime," but later reports named only Bradley.

Bradley was found guilty of first-degree murder at Lovingston and sentenced to hang. He was hanged there on January 30, 1904, after writing a statement in which he admitted the killing. No report of the release of Young and Murphey was found.

The story began as a special to the Richmond Times-Dispatch, which headlined it "Mysterious Death on Moving Train" with the deck "Two Negroes Under Arrest and in Danger of Lynching." The same paper's front-page digest put the point more directly: the suspects "were not returned to Gladstone for fear of lynching." The Alexandria Gazette, the Savannah Morning News, and the Raleigh News & Observer reprinted the text, the last two through the Associated Press, under headlines about the killing such as "Crack! Crack! Over the Roar."

None of these papers commented on the crowd beyond the closing "Trouble is feared," and the Washington Times ran only the account of the killing. The follow-up coverage centered on Bradley, whom the Times-Dispatch called "a negro tramp and desperado." No coverage of the episode was found in the Black press.

The September reports dated the killing to the early morning of Friday, September 11, while the reports of Bradley's hanging gave September 10. The men's names also varied in print, appearing as "Lawrence Young" in the News & Observer and "Low Young" in the September 14 dispatch.

accounts.label: Lynchburg special (wire report)
accounts.gist: Harris was found shot dead on a freight car at Gladstone; two Black men who had been at Gladstone were arrested in Lynchburg on suspicion, and a crowd of several hundred waited at Gladstone for them while Lynchburg authorities refused to send them; 'Trouble is feared.'

accounts.label: Detective's case against Bradley
accounts.gist: A Baldwin agency detective said Frank Bradley rode the freight with Harris after a night of drinking in Richmond and carried a revolver with cartridges bought to replace those fired; Bradley denied the killing and blamed a man in overalls.

accounts.label: Lynchburg dispatch, Sept. 14
accounts.gist: Nelson authorities were looking for Bradley, said to have been with Young and Murphy, who had 'been arrested for the crime.'

accounts.label: Bradley's confession
accounts.gist: Before his hanging Bradley left a written statement saying he was guilty and sorry he had killed the man.

framing.detail: The Times-Dispatch headlined 'Mysterious Death on Moving Train' with the deck 'Two Negroes Under Arrest and in Danger of Lynching' and called the killing a 'dark tragedy' 'wrapped in mystery'.

Out-of-state papers ran the wire text under headlines about the killing ('Crack! Crack! Over the Roar', 'By an Unknown Hand Bridgeman Was Slain'), keeping 'Trouble is feared' without comment on the crowd.
The Times-Dispatch's front-page digest summarized the story as suspects 'not returned to Gladstone for fear of lynching.'
The follow-up called Bradley 'a negro tramp and desperado' and said the detective's evidence was 'of a very damaging character'.

conflicts.note: Spelling variants of the same two men; the Lynchburg special (A3) is the original text.
The September reports were written the day of the killing; the January reports may be counting the night before.
